title: GPU runtime profiling deep dive with Hyperion Systems
customer_attendees: Derek Lawson - Head of ML Infra
next_steps: Redwood: share kernel-selection benchmark spreadsheet and raw perf traces
Customer: provide representative model weights and 1-2 sample prompts/datasets
Schedule on-prem pilot provision (Hyperion infra team + Redwood SE) for Jan 10
Send SOC2 + KMS integration notes and network diagrams
action_items: Maya Patel: run CUDA-graph vs non-CUDA-graph end-to-end for 2k context, batch sizes 1/4/8 (due: 2027-01-06)
Derek Lawson: share internal model flavor, quantization preferences, and sample input distribution (due: 2026-12-31)
Jonas Li: confirm firewall/NAT rules for VPC peering and provide egress IPs (due: 2027-01-05)
summary: Redwood SE team walked Hyperion through GPU runtime profiling methodology focusing on kernel selection, TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM tradeoffs, CUDA graph benefits, KV cache behavior, batching and quantization impacts, and VPC/on-prem constraints.

Customer is evaluating Dedicated vs Private deployment for latency-sensitive inference across 4k token flows; main concerns: deterministic latency, cost per token, and secure KMS integration for weights and logs.
topics: CUDA graphs effects on first-token latency and steady-state throughput
KV cache eviction and prefix caching
Batching strategies for mixed request sizes
Quantization impacts on perf and quality
transcript: [00:00] Avery Chen: alright hey everybody thanks for making time, this is Avery from Redwood, i'll let maya intro herself and then we can jump in to the perf stuff
[00:08] Maya Patel: hi all Maya, I'm the SE, we'll run through some profiling results and then do a live trace walkthrough, quick note transcription might be a bit off for acronyms, sorry in advance

[00:15] Derek Lawson: thanks, appreciate it, i invited priya and jorge cause they'll own the infra side, we're looking at steady latencies under 200ms for short completions and predictable tails for 4k contexts
[00:28] Priya Singh: and cost is big too — we need to compare dedicated reserved nodes vs private on-prem; quantization options might help but we worry about accuracy drop
[00:40] Jonas Li: quick Q — are we assuming same hardware? hyperion uses A100S 80GB and some T4s for edge, want to see how kernels pick across GPUs
[00:50] Maya Patel: yes we profiled on A100S, and also a smaller run on RTX6000 series to show kernel selection differences — big difference in Tensor cores availability changes kernel pathing
[01:05] Avery Chen: goal today: show where time is going (compute vs memcpy vs kernel launch), how CUDA graphs reduce launch overheads, and where TensorRT-LLM wins/loses vs vLLM for your workloads
[01:18] Jorge Ramos: good, also please surface KV cache consistency — we have streaming scenarios and cache hits need to be near 100% for perf
[01:25] Maya Patel: totally, we'll show prefix caching and KV hit/miss curves with varying request shapes

[02:05] [screen share begins] Maya Patel: here's the profiler timeline — you can see spikes at token 0, that's kernel warmup + kernel selection path where runtime probes model shapes and picks a kernel variant
[02:20] Derek Lawson: that initial spike is our concern, for short responses it's a big fraction of latency, can you smooth that?

[02:28] Maya Patel: two levers: CUDA graphs to capture recurrent patterns so first-token amortized cost is lower, and pre-warming with a tiny synthetic request (prefill) to initialize kernels and allocate KV caches
[02:45] Maya Patel: note though cudagraphs slightly ties you to a particular input shape/seq len; we use graph families and fallback to dynamic paths when shape deviates (at cost) — so tradeoff there
[03:00] Priya Singh: graph families? can you elaborate

[03:05] Maya Patel: sure — we compile a few CUDA graphs for common sequence lengths like 32, 256, 1024, and route live requests to the nearest graph; for outliers we run dynamic kernels which are slower but rare
[03:22] Derek Lawson: hmm ok, in our traffic 20% of requests are long tails (2k-4k) — that sounds nontrivial

[03:28] Samira Noor: right, that's where KV cache comes in — if you're streaming and appending, we keep a KV cache so the per-step work is reduced; but bigger context increases memory pressure and kernel choice changes to memory-bound paths
[03:45] Jonas Li: what about kernel selection heuristics? we saw runtime pick naive GEMM kernels sometimes instead of split-k or fused kernels

[03:53] Maya Patel: good catch — runtime uses model dtypes, hidden size, seq len, and hardware capability to pick among fused attention, flash-attention variants, and TensorRT fused transformer ops; sometimes heuristics favor stability (less numerical diff) over fastest kernel — we can tune thresholds
[04:12] Derek Lawson: can Redwood adjust that per-customer? we need determinism for SLAs
[04:18] Avery Chen: yes, we can pin kernel policies per deployment (dedicated/private) — there's a profile config that sets aggressive perf optimization vs conservative numerics
[04:30] Priya Singh: and how do TensorRT-LLM and vLLM compare overall? for throughput and latency

[04:36] Maya Patel: summarized: TensorRT-LLM wins on steady-state throughput for fp16/INT8 quant models due to aggressive fusion and TensorRT kernels; vLLM often has lower-first-token latency because of lighter dynamic paths, but less kernel fusion means lower steady throughput for large batches

[04:56] Samira Noor: caveat — TensorRT-LLM requires more compilation time and may need to regenerate engines when you change prompt templates or sequence lengths often, so for highly dynamic workloads vLLM's dynamic kernel path can be preferable
[05:12] Derek Lawson: any numbers? even ballpark helps

[05:18] Maya Patel: on A100S, for a 2k context, batch size 1, 512 hidden model: vLLM path did ~30 tokens/s steady (with kv caching), TensorRT-LLM tuned fp16 ran ~55 tokens/s steady but first-token time was 220ms vs vLLM 120ms before warmup; with CUDA graphs TensorRT first-token drops to ~140ms
[05:40] Priya Singh: interesting, so cudagraphs halves the warmup gap roughly
[05:44] Maya Patel: in our traces yes, because the graph captures kernel launches and avoids per-launch overheads; it's not magic — still depends on shape alignment
[05:52] Jonas Li: and INT8 quantization? any perf/quality numbers

[05:56] Samira Noor: INT8 on TensorRT-LLM gave ~1.8-2.2x throughput vs fp16 on some ops but quality degradation was model-dependent; we run eval prompts and perplexity/metric deltas to decide acceptable thresholds
[06:12] Derek Lawson: so policy: do we keep fp16 in prod and test INT8 for non-critical customers?
[06:18] Avery Chen: that's a common pattern — dedicated clusters for prod keep fp16 with conservative kernels; we run canary INT8 on shadow traffic to verify quality regression limits
[06:30] Priya Singh: about KV cache eviction — we saw misses in our streaming tests and that spiked tail latencies

[06:36] Maya Patel: yes, evictions usually happen when model state grows beyond allocated KV capacity or when we evict due to LRU policy during multi-tenant spikes; Redwood can configure KV cache sizing per route and we also have adaptive eviction heuristics that favor hot prefixes
[06:58] Derek Lawson: will we be able to pin KV memory to avoid eviction during critical windows?
[07:03] Maya Patel: in Dedicated/Private yes, you can reserve memory lanes for specific customers/routes so the runtime prioritizes them — good for SLAs
[07:12] Jorge Ramos: networking question — for Private deployment we will put Redwood's control plane in our VPC, what about KMS and logs?
[07:20] Avery Chen: we support customer-managed KMS (AWS KMS, HashiCorp Vault, HSM) for key wraps; audit logs can be forwarded to your SIEM via S3 or syslog; we'll share the integration doc
[07:32] Priya Singh: any perf overhead for KMS envelope decrypt at startup?
[07:36] Maya Patel: negligible at inference time — keys are used to unwrap model keys at model load; we keep decrypted keys in memory in a secure enclave until model unload, no per-token KMS calls

[07:52] [screen share: kernel-selection table] Maya Patel: here's where runtime switched from flash-attn to split-k for long sequences, see memcpy+transpose overhead increases, that's why we sometimes favour a memory-bound kernel
[08:10] Derek Lawson: can you annotate which kernels are deterministic numerically? our QA needs reproducible outputs

[08:16] Samira Noor: yes we tag kernels with "stability" and "determinism" scores; fused TF ops sometimes slightly change fp rounding but within tolerance, we can pin conservative kernels for reproducibility
[08:34] Maya Patel: demo time — i'll open a perf trace, note the timeline markers for model load, prefill, token 0, and token steady state
[08:50] [long pause as demo loads]
[09:30] Maya Patel: here is a raw trace: compute time 60%, memcpy 20%, kernel launch overhead 15%, miscellaneous 5% — with CUDA graphs kernel launch overhead drops to ~3% and memcpy stays similar
[09:50] Priya Singh: does cudagraphs affect memory fragmentation?
[09:55] Jonas Li: good question, we saw fragmentation on long-lived graphs if not carefully freed
[10:02] Maya Patel: yes, graph replay can hold onto allocations, we garbage collect graphs on epoch boundaries and have a compacting allocator to mitigate fragmentation
[10:18] Derek Lawson: for on-prem, what's involved to run the profiling agent?

[10:24] Avery Chen: we provide a lightweight trace agent that runs as a privileged daemon collecting nvtx and profiling events, it uploads traces to your S3 or to a customer-managed bucket; for air-gapped we provide an offline bundle
[10:40] Priya Singh: security note: offline bundle ok but need signed artifacts and reproducible builds
[10:46] Samira Noor: agreed, we sign agent binaries and provide checksums; we'll share the release process doc
[11:05] Derek Lawson: any recommended batching strategy for mixed sizes? our traffic has 70% small requests, 30% large streaming ones

[11:12] Maya Patel: hybrid strategy: immediate path for small low-latency requests (batch size 1 w/ KV cache hot), and queued micro-batching for medium requests with timeout heuristics; for large streaming we keep them on dedicated lanes or different VM pools to avoid head-of-line blocking
[11:32] Priya Singh: and autoscaling concerns? bursty traffic created noisy-neighbor issues in our tests
[11:38] Jonas Li: we saw GPU oversubscription when autoscale failed to spin up dedicated nodes quickly
[11:44] Maya Patel: Redwood Dedicated supports predictive autoscaling with warm pools and burst capacity; for Private we recommend a small reserved buffer for critical routes
[12:00] Derek Lawson: curious about multi-tenant vs single-tenant perf delta on A100S

[12:06] Maya Patel: multi-tenant can introduce jitter if KV cache memory is oversubscribed and kernels get warmed/unwarmed; single-tenant gives best tail and deterministic behavior at cost of utilization
[12:20] Priya Singh: action items recap please

[12:24] Avery Chen: recap: we'll share kernel-selection spreadsheet and traces; Maya to run cudagraph vs non-cudagraph experiments; Hyperion to share models and input distro; Jonas to provide networking details; schedule pilot Jan 10
[12:36] Jorge Ramos: thanks everyone, this was helpful, we'll circle back after we look at the traces
[12:40] [call ends]
